Question_text: A group of students performs an experiment to investigate the flow of oil at different temperatures. 200 cm³ of oil is heated gently and its temperature θ is recorded. The oil is then poured through a funnel into a second beaker, as shown in Fig. 1.1. The time t taken for the oil to flow through the funnel is recorded with a stopwatch.
image: Fig. 1.1 shows an experimental setup for measuring the flow time of oil. A funnel is suspended over a beaker. Oil is being poured from an upper beaker (labeled 'beaker') into the funnel. The funnel has a narrow spout through which the oil flows into a lower beaker (also labeled 'beaker'). The oil is clearly visible in the upper beaker, funnel, and lower beaker, indicating the flow path.

Parts.part_text: State why it is important to stir the oil during heating.
Explain why the oil is heated gently.
On Fig. 1.3, plot the graph of t/s on the y-axis against θ/°C on the x-axis. Start your graph from θ = 0°C and t = 12s. Draw the curved line of best fit.
Parts.image: Fig. 1.2 shows a table with two columns: θ/°C and t/s, containing experimental data. The data points are (69, 13.69), (52, 14.97), (35, 17.34), (24, 21.16), (17, 25.16), (10, 28.85). Fig 1.3 is an empty grid with an x-axis labeled θ/°C and a y-axis labeled t/s, with the origin starting at 0 and 12 respectively. This grid is for plotting the graph.

Parts.part_text: Estimate the time taken for oil at 80 °C to flow through the funnel.
State the maximum reading on a standard laboratory liquid-in-glass thermometer that is suitable for this experiment.
Explain why it is not possible to repeat a reading immediately after it is taken.

Tick two boxes to show which of the following will make the experiment more accurate. Options are: using a more sensitive thermometer, using two people to take the measurements, using a thicker oil, using a larger range of readings, pouring the oil quickly after taking its temperature.

Question_text: Fig. 2.1 shows a wooden metre rule with small holes drilled through it. The metre rule is suspended from the hole at 5.0cm so that it can swing freely, as shown in Fig. 2.2. The rule is made to swing from side-to-side and the time T for one complete swing is determined.
image: Fig. 2.1 shows a top-down view of a wooden metre rule, marked from 0 to 100 cm. Small holes are drilled at various points along its length, with one specifically labeled 'holes' near the 90cm mark. Fig. 2.2 shows the metre rule suspended vertically from a pivot (represented by a short horizontal line intersecting the rule near its top end, around the 5cm mark based on the text). An arrow indicates the rule swinging from side-to-side, forming an arc.

Parts.part_text: Describe three experimental techniques used to obtain an accurate value for T.
Describe how T varies with d.
Parts.image: Fig. 2.3 shows a table with two columns: d/cm and T/s. The data points are (5.0, 1.61), (10.0, 1.57), (20.0, 1.52), (30.0, 1.58), (40.0, 1.91).

Parts.part_text: Suggest the value of T for d = 95.0 cm.
Suggest why T was not measured for d = 50.0 cm.

Question_text: The efficiency of a motor is measured using the apparatus shown in Fig. 3.1. When the motor is switched on, the string winds round the pulley and the load is lifted. Six students measure the time t taken for the load to be lifted a height h of 1.0m.
image: Fig. 3.1 (not to scale) depicts an experimental setup. A motor is placed horizontally with its shaft connected to a pulley. A string is wound around the pulley and extends downwards, attached to a load at its other end. The load rests on the ground. A vertical arrow indicates the height 'h = 1.0 m' from the ground to the point where the string leaves the pulley. The motor is connected to a 'power supply'.

Parts.part_text: The result of 5.92 s is discarded. Suggest why this result is very much larger than the others.
Calculate the average time t_av of the other results. Considering the variation in the students' results, give your answer to an appropriate number of significant figures. Show your working.
The efficiency E of the motor is given by the relationship E = (2 x 10^2) / (3 x t_av) %. Use this relationship to calculate E.
Describe one way in which the students can measure h accurately.

Question_text: A student performs an experiment using optical pins to find the effect of a circular transparent plastic block, on parallel rays of light. Fig. 4.1 shows the circular plastic block on a sheet of white paper. The student draws round the block with a sharp pencil. The student also draws three parallel lines up to the block before starting the experiment.
image: Fig. 4.1 shows a circular plastic block drawn on a sheet of paper. Three parallel lines (line 1, line 2, line 3) are drawn leading up to the bottom edge of the circle. Pins P1 and P2 are marked on line 1, before it reaches the circle. Pins P3 and P4 are marked above the circle, in line with the expected emergent ray from line 1 if refracted. A dashed line passes through the center of the circle, perpendicular to the incident rays and aligned with line 2, indicating the normal for line 2. The block is labeled 'circular plastic block'.

Parts.part_text: Explain why the student draws round the block.
The student places pins P₁ and P₂ on line 1, representing an incident ray of light. Describe how the student places pins P₃ and P₄ to locate the emergent ray.
complete the path of the ray along line 1 through the block,
draw the normal at the point where the ray along line 1 enters the block,
measure the angle of incidence i where the ray along line 1 enters the block.
Explain why a ray along line 2 passes through the block without changing direction.
On Fig. 4.1, complete the path of a ray along line 3 through the block.
